items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Improving Transparency and Reliability in Automated Decision-Making Systems
items.abstract: Automated decision-making systems increasingly influence healthcare, finance, recruitment, education, public administration, and digital platforms. Although advanced machine-learning models can discover complex relationships, their opaque reasoning can obstruct auditing, contestability, and safe deployment. This narrative review examines how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) may improve transparency and reliability by clarifying model behavior, revealing data dependencies, supporting error detection, and enabling informed human oversight. It synthesizes established work on interpretable modeling, local feature attribution, surrogate explanations, counterfactual reasoning, explanation evaluation, and governance. A conceptual assurance framework connects data provenance, predictive validation, explanation fidelity, subgroup analysis, and operational monitoring. The paper distinguishes understandable explanations from evidence that a system is accurate, robust, or fair: an attractive explanation alone does not establish reliability. A non-empirical diagram illustrates complementary assurance dimensions without implying measured results. Practical implications include tailoring explanations to decision recipients, testing explanation stability under perturbations, documenting uncertainty, and establishing appeal mechanisms. The review concludes that XAI is most effective when embedded within a wider socio-technical accountability process rather than deployed as a stand-alone visualization technique.

items.title: Explainable CatBoost–TabPFN Hybrid for Mode-Resolved Interlaminar Fracture Toughness Prediction in Fiber-Reinforced Polymer Composites
items.abstract: Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites offer high specific strength, high stiffness, and good corrosion resistance, which makes them suitable for aerospace, automotive, marine, and wind-energy structures. Their interlaminar fracture behavior is harder to pin down because delamination testing is slow and costly and the response shifts with loading mode. This study presents an explainable hybrid machine learning framework for interlaminar fracture toughness under Mode-I, Mode-II, and Mixed-Mode loading. A weighted ensemble pairs Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), a gradient-boosting method, with the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN), a pretrained transformer built for tabular data. A Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) tunes the CatBoost hyperparameters and the ensemble weight against specimen-grouped cross-validation. The work draws on the public D-STANDART experimental dataset and treats DCB, ELS, and MMB as three separate prediction problems for GIC, GIIC, and GC rather than pooling them into one model. The analyzed D-STANDART specimens comprise pultruded carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) material based on Zoltek PX35 carbon fiber. The data are partitioned at the specimen level, so no specimen contributes records to more than one subset, and feature selection uses the training data alone. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) then measure how each input shifts the predicted toughness in each mode. The framework reached an R2 of 0.9280 for DCB, 0.9870 for ELS, and 0.9627 for MMB, with RMSE values of 5.1759, 1.5041, and 2.8809 and MAE values of 1.6502, 0.5372, and 0.7000, respectively. Bringing a tabular foundation model into delamination analysis, and keeping the three loading modes apart, lets the framework report mode-specific feature behavior instead of one averaged picture.

items.title: Exploring Mongolian Trilingual Students’ Perceptions About Academic and Affective Impacts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technologies: A Descriptive Qualitative Study
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into education has received increasing attention over the past couple of years. However, the perceived impacts of such technologies by trilingual learners have remained unaddressed by scholars. Compared with conventional second or foreign language learners, trilingual learners may need to coordinate languages with different levels of proficiency and functions while also coping with unequal AI support across languages. To fill the gap, this descriptive qualitative study drew on technology acceptance model (TAM) and control‐value theory (CVT) to examine Mongolian trilingual learners’ perceptions about the academic and affective impacts of AI tools. A sample of 40 Mongolian trilingual students in Inner Mongolia, China were asked to complete an open‐ended questionnaire and attend an interview. The results of thematic analysis demonstrated that AI technologies had imposed several positive and negative academic and affective impacts on trilingual students. Particularly, it was found that AI adoption could improve learning efficiency, autonomy, and agency, but over‐reliance on AI tools might lead to dependency, plagiarism acts, surface learning, and reduced critical thinking. Regarding affective consequences, the students found AI adoption exciting, motivating, and emotionally safe, while they endorsed the possibility of anxiety, stress, fear, emotional tension, and emotional detachment. The study discusses the findings and provides practical implications for trilingual teachers, students, and policymakers by enhancing their AI and emotional literacy.

items.title: EXPRESS: From Chit-Chat to Conversion: Cost-Efficient Conversational Recommendation via Retrospective Learning and Isolated Reflection
items.abstract: Conversational recommendation systems help digital platforms elicit user preferences through multi-turn interaction, but they often face a practical tension between recommendation accuracy and interaction cost when users provide vague or low-information inputs. This study follows a design science approach to develop a cost-conscious conversational recommendation artifact for such ambiguous service encounters. The artifact is guided by two design principles. First, retrospective outcome-guided supervision uses successful historical conversion trajectories as downstream anchors for improving responses at earlier low-information states. Second, isolated reflection separates recommendation generation from consistency checking, enabling diagnostic regeneration when candidate responses conflict with previously stated user constraints. In implementation, the artifact instantiates these principles through parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source large language models and prompt-isolated role switching over a shared backbone model. We validate the artifact on three conversational recommendation datasets covering movie and e-commerce settings, using outcome efficacy, interaction efficiency, process analysis, ablation analysis, robustness checks, and human evaluation. Here, interaction efficiency refers to user-visible dialogue turns, while computational burden is reported separately through training, memory, and latency measurements. The empirical results show that the artifact improves recommendation effectiveness while maintaining a favorable balance between interaction burden and conversion outcomes under the tested conditions. Process-level analysis further characterizes how recommendation behavior evolves over the course of dialogue. This study contributes transferable design principles for embedding retrospective preference optimization and isolated reflection into conversational recommendation systems, offering operational guidance for platforms seeking to improve personalization under constraints on interaction cost.

items.title: FacilityAudit-Agent: Beyond Mention-as-Usage for Fine-Grained Facility Contribution Attribution in Astrophysics Publications
items.abstract: Observatory bibliographies increasingly need to determine not only whether a facility is named in a paper, but how its data support the scientific argument. We frame this need as semantic contribution attribution on a six-level scale (L0-L5), from non-use and mention-only cases to auxiliary, major, and exclusive data support. We present FacilityAudit-Agent, a framework that builds a page-bounded outline of each PDF, enriches sections with roles and facility mentions, and uses a tool-calling large language model (LLM) to fetch text on demand. Evidence from the sections is combined through an explicit decision tree and a coverage-calibrated confidence score, with uncertain cases routed to human review. The framework supports both single-facility and inventory audits and transfers to new facilities without retraining. On a test set of 39,358 human-annotated paper-facility pairs, FacilityAudit-Agent achieves 89.1% accuracy and 79.8% macro-F1 in single_audit mode, outperforming the other three baselines by 5.8, 8.3, and 12.1 accuracy points, respectively, with the clearest gains at L2 and L5. In inventory_audit mode, it also leads in facility listing and in level assignment among listed pairs. Ablations show multi-hop reading and tree indexing matter most for L3-L5. FacilityAudit-Agent has been deployed at the National Astronomical Data Center, where it is responsible for processing publications related to LAMOST, FAST, and EP.

items.title: Factors influencing registered nurses’ attitudes toward and literacy in artificial intelligence: a cross-sectional systematic review
items.abstract: Background Presently, artificial intelligence technology is being extensively applied across clinical nursing practice. However, whether this technology can be deeply integrated into clinical workflows depends largely on nurses’ attitudes and literacy regarding artificial intelligence. Consequently, conducting an in depth exploration of core factors shaping registered nurses’ artificial intelligence attitudes and literacy holds significant importance for driving the rapid development of intelligent nursing. Methods This study strictly adhered to PRISMA guidelines. Systematic searches were conducted across seven English databases, namely PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, The Cochrane Library, IEEE Xplore, and CINAHL, alongside three Chinese databases, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, and VIP Database. The search timeframe ranged from database inception through May 30, 2026. Following screening according to inclusion and exclusion criteria, independent factors influencing attitudes and literacy were extracted. Employing a narrative synthesis approach, these influencing factors were categorized, summarized, and narratively integrated across distinct thematic domains. Results A total of 30 studies involving 12,958 registered nurses were included in this systematic review. The majority of the studies were conducted in China and Turkey. The independent factors influencing registered nurses’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence included educational attainment, age, length of service, gender, professional title/nursing level, hospital tier/category, AI awareness/understanding/knowledge, AI training experience, AI usage experience, artificial intelligence anxiety, and digital leadership. The factors independently affecting nurses’ artificial intelligence literacy included leadership style, AI training experience, and usage experience/frequency. Conclusion Current evidence indicates that key modifiable factors to improve nurses’ attitudes toward and literacy in artificial intelligence include AI-related training, practical hands-on experience, and organizational leadership, while technical anxiety should not be overlooked. Compared with demographic characteristics, educational and experiential interventions appear more effective in enhancing nurses’ artificial intelligence literacy levels. Nursing managers should actively implement smart training programs, increase opportunities for nurses to apply new technologies in clinical practice, and formulate relevant policies regarding data privacy protection and accountability division, thereby promoting the safe and effective integration of AI technology into patient care. items.title: Fast and Useful: Adapting Distilled Generators for Visual Learning
items.abstract: Distilled text-to-image models generate images quickly, but classifiers trained on those images can perform substantially worse than classifiers trained on images from their slower base models. We adapt released distilled generators to produce better training data while retaining fast generation. We fit a low-rank update to the student's first prediction so that it reaches an intermediate state produced by its unguided base, then disable the update and let the unchanged student finish generation. The base supplies training targets and is absent at inference. Guided targets and shorter jumps give classifiers lower accuracy in our ablations, showing why the state used for supervision matters. Across three generator families, the adapted images train better classifiers than images from the released students. With class-name templates at full ImageNet-1k scale, ResNet-50 top-1 rises from 8.4% to 34.2% for FLUX.2-klein and from 12.7% to 32.1% for SD-Turbo, using two and three denoiser evaluations per image, respectively. Fixed adapters also improve results on additional classes, fine-grained datasets, and other learner architectures and training recipes. Template-based adaptation remains useful against richer-prompt alternatives, while the benefit of combining adaptation with LLM generation prompts depends on the generator. Adapting a single generation step makes fast generators substantially more useful for training visual models.

items.title: Fear-Specific Technophobia as a Mediator Between Daily Technical Support and Instrumental Versus Hedonic Technology Use in Later Life: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships. Objective This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI. Results DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229; P <.001) but did not significantly affect fear of personal failure ( P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009; P =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116). Conclusions DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.

items.title: Fintech-Driven Transformation of Financial Markets and Investment Decision-Making: A Conceptual Study
items.abstract: Financial technology (fintech) is changing how financial markets operate and how investors access, interpret, and act on financial information. Digital payments, mobile investment platforms, robo-advisory services, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, big-data analytics, blockchain, and automated trading have altered the speed, reach, and informational basis of financial decisions. Yet the consequences are not uniformly beneficial: greater access and analytical capacity can coexist with cyber risk, algorithmic opacity, behavioural overconfidence, platform dependence, and unequal digital capabilities. This conceptual study synthesizes the literature review supplied for the paper, which covers fintech adoption, digital transformation in financial services, capital-market infrastructure, AI-supported investment decisions, financial risk management, mutual-fund choice, and the behavioural implications of personal-finance applications. The study proposes an integrated conceptual model linking fintech capabilities to investment decision-making quality through information accessibility, analytical support, transaction efficiency, and trust. Behavioural biases act as mediators, while financial literacy, digital capability, and governance quality moderate the proposed relationships. Expected outcomes include decision quality, portfolio alignment, participation, and market efficiency, subject to risks and institutional conditions. The model is conceptual and is not presented as empirically validated. It offers propositions for future testing and practical implications for investors, fintech providers, financial institutions, and regulators. The central argument is that fintech creates value when technological capability is combined with informed users, transparent design, robust safeguards, and meaningful human oversight.

items.title: FIRE SIMULATION AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF DIGITAL SCENARIOS FOR FIREFIGHTING AND RESCUE TRAINING AND COMMAND
items.abstract: Digital transformation is opening new avenues for innovating fire fighting and rescue training, drills, and command operations, steering them toward visualization, data-driven methodologies, and measurability. This article analyzes the scientific foundations and practical applications of fire simulation, digital scenarios, virtual reality, augmented reality, and digital twins in enhancing situational awareness, tactical decision-making, and inter-agency coordination capabilities. Building on this framework, the paper proposes key solutions, including establishing a digital scenario bank, standardizing scenario structures, integrating digital simulations with field-based training, developing command simulation training centers, and building digital capabilities for instructors, officers, and firefighters.

items.title: FOCUS: A Lightweight Mamba-2 Model for EEG-Based Cognitive Workload Classification
items.abstract: Cognitive workload estimation from physiological signals is increasingly relevant in high-risk environments, where continuous and unobtrusive monitoring can inform adaptive systems and safety interventions. This paper presents FOCUS (Frequency-band Optimized Cognitive-load Ultralight SSM), a compact Mamba-2-based model for EEG-based binary workload classification under constrained data conditions. Rather than learning frequency sensitivity from data, FOCUS encodes preprocessed multi-channel EEG using a fixed FFT decomposition that covers the five canonical EEG bands. The proposed model combines depthwise-separable convolution and a weight-shared encoder-bottleneck Mamba-2 pair, with 0.04 million parameters and 0.11 GFLOPs. Evaluated in a pilot study with 11 participants under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation across three cognitively distinct tasks, FOCUS achieves 74.75% accuracy on the full dataset at 0.08 ms GPU model-forward latency. In the weight-sharing ablation, the shared configuration achieves 4.55 percentage points higher accuracy on the full dataset than the non-shared variant while reducing the SSM parameter budget; however, this difference does not reach statistical significance under a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test ($p=0.083$). Overall, the selected FOCUS configuration provides a favorable trade-off between classification performance and computational cost within this controlled pilot setting.

items.title: Foundation model-driven framework for human–object interaction prediction with segmentation mask integration
items.abstract: Abstract In this work, we introduce Segmentation to Human–Object Interaction (Seg2HOI), a novel framework that integrates segmentation-based vision foundation models with the human–object interaction (HOI) task, distinguished from traditional detection-based HOI methods. Our approach enhances HOI detection by not only predicting the standard triplets but also introducing quadruplets, which extend HOI triplets by including segmentation masks for human–object pairs. More specifically, Seg2HOI inherits the properties of the vision foundation model (e.g., promptable and interactive mechanisms) and incorporates an implicit relation-learning decoder that applies these attributes to the HOI task. By freezing the vision foundation model, Seg2HOI preserves its original capabilities while using pixel-level mask guidance to support high-level relational reasoning. Despite being trained only for the HOI task, without additional training mechanisms for these properties, the framework demonstrates that such features still operate efficiently. Extensive experiments on two public benchmark datasets demonstrate that Seg2HOI achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, even in zero-shot scenarios. Lastly, we propose that Seg2HOI can generate HOI quadruplets and interactive HOI segmentation from novel text and visual prompts that were not used during training, making it versatile for a wide range of applications by leveraging this flexibility.

items.title: Foundation Models Meet Power Grid Topology for Cascade Prediction
items.abstract: Accurate early-stage prediction of cascading failure severity is essential for assessing the vulnerability of power transmission networks. However, existing data-driven approaches often rely on network-specific representations, limiting their generalizability across power system topologies. This work investigates the complementary capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for cascading failure severity prediction. First, standalone LLM predictors are developed using a LoRA-fine-tuned LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct model with varying degrees of topological information. A hybrid Graph-LLM fusion framework is then proposed, integrating a Topology-Aware Graph Attention Transformer (TAGAT) with the LLM through confidence-gated fusion. TAGAT captures structural dependencies among transmission lines, while the LLM extracts representations from early-stage power-flow observations and aggregated cascade descriptors. The frameworks are evaluated on 30,000 simulated cascading failure scenarios for each of the IEEE 118-bus and IEEE 300-bus systems. Using only the first four cascade steps, the hybrid framework achieves weighted F1 scores of 0.94 and 0.92, respectively. In cross-system transfer from IEEE 118-bus to IEEE 300-bus, it achieves 0.72 zero-shot accuracy, improving to 0.83 with limited target-system calibration, outperforming standalone models and conventional baselines. These results show the potential of combining graph-based structural learning with foundation models to improve cascading failure severity prediction and cross-system transferability.

items.title: Four Null Causal Spacetime
items.abstract: This research presents a comprehensive synthesis of the principal mathematical, computational, and theoretical achievements of the Four Null Causal Spacetime research program. The research begins with a foundational question: Can four future directed lightlike vectors, arranged in regular tetrahedral spatial directions, provide the causal structure from which four dimensional spacetime geometry and its physical interactions can be reconstructed? Starting from this geometric construction, the program investigates connections between Lorentzian spacetime, general relativity, discrete gravity, electromagnetism, gravitational waves, causal propagation, and quantum field theory. The article reviews the development of the research through Parts I–XVII and the integrated research updates of 22 October 2026. Its principal topics and reported achievements include: Foundational geometry: Exact tetrahedral incidence identities, complementary three dimensional gradient and circulation sectors, Hodge duality exchange, and Lorentzian metric reconstruction from four null generators. Discrete gravity: A four-dimensional parallelotope subdivided into 24 four simplices, with 15 edge variables decomposed into ten metric components and five auxiliary directions. Einstein gravity correspondence: Recovery of the Fierz Pauli operator, two physical gravitational wave polarizations, Newtonian gravity, and standard weak-field PPN coefficients within the stated assumptions. Nonlinear gravitational interactions: Exact agreement in 1,440,000 coefficient comparisons for the leading Einstein cubic interaction, together with additional numerical quartic correspondence tests. Gravitational stability: Identification of an unstable microscopic scalar mode with growth magnitude approximately 2.890053638, motivating the development of Formulation A. Characteristic null dynamics: A constrained null ray architecture incorporating radiative shear, scalar and vector constraints, relational time, and a stable free spin 2 sector. Electromagnetism and quantum universality: Independent Maxwell discretizations with matching infrared photon properties, gauge identities, scalar QED infrared behavior, and leading gravity photon coupling. Causal propagation: Computational tests of conserved gravitational curvature disturbances propagating within the relativistic future light cone. Null boundary geometry: Canonical area boost variables, exact cancellation of internal edge contributions under matched null ray gluing, and connections with published null gravity formulations. Quantum gravity connections: Exact four simplex combinatorial correspondences, semiclassical group field theory compatibility, a leading soft-graviton factorization theorem candidate, and a partial covariant effective field theory gauge completion construction. The essay also examines unsuccessful approaches, mathematical limitations, and unresolved physical questions. In particular, a complete stable nonlinear microscopic gravitational evolution law and a fully derived quantum theory of gravity have not yet been established. Its results have different levels of support, including exact mathematical identities within specified constructions, computationally tested correspondences, numerical benchmarks, conditional arguments, and provisional theorem candidates. Artificial intelligence tools contributed extensively to the research process, including mathematical derivations, symbolic and numerical computations, computational testing, literature analysis, scientific interpretation, and manuscript preparation. Related Research Record The full mathematical and computational development is consolidated in: Gurbuz Dolu, Four Null Causal Spacetime: Complete Master Edition, 164 pages, 22 October 2026. Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/23581934 The Complete Master Edition serves as the principal internal research reference for the synthesis. The essay provides an accessible overview of the program's achievements, scientific reasoning, limitations, and outstanding questions. items.title: From archive to resource: bringing legacy data back to life at scale with large language models
items.abstract: Pharmaceutical companies maintain vast archives of legacy preclinical study reports that contain study-context details, such as fasting, anesthesia, and laboratory instrumentation, that are rarely captured in structured data formats, yet they can correlate with clinical pathology parameters values and limit the reuse of historical data. This work demonstrates practical, scalable solutions to recover such descriptors from heterogeneous report texts using large language model (LLM)-based extraction pipelines developed independently by two industry teams. The pipelines identify and normalize metadata fields and return verbatim evidence with page and section reference, hasting human verification and iterative refinement. Evaluation of over 400 documents against expert-curated reference values showed high agreement across a broad set of metadata fields. Performance was strongest for consistently reported items and lower for descriptors subject to linguistic or report structure variability. Extraction time has shrunk from 25 minutes in the manual benchmark to 1.6 minutes. As a concrete biological demonstration, we show that fasting status extracted from report text was associated with species- and analyte-specific shifts in clinical chemistry parameters, illustrating how recovered metadata can improve selection of historical controls. Key strengths of the approach are scalability, traceability, and the ability to recover information missing from current industry standards. Main limitations are dependence on source-report quality and initial expert effort to define and refine schemas. These results establish how LLMs can convert heterogeneous, unstructured legacy reports into evidence-grounded, reusable and structured metadata, leading to better experimental comparability, and thus enabling reliable data pooling or informed virtual control selection.

items.title: From Atoms to Reactors: A Critical Review of a Decade of Machine Learning in Heterogeneous Catalysis (2017–2026)
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This critical review traces the evolution of machine learning (ML) across the full value chain of heterogeneous catalysis over 2017–2026, from catalyst discovery to reactor and process design, and across the principal reaction families (CO 2 reduction, water splitting, nitrogen chemistry, zeolite‐catalyzed transformations). Each stage is evaluated against four criteria — data foundation, method maturity, experimental validation and deployment readiness — through a structured capability scorecard. Digitalization has advanced from the top of the length scale downward: prediction of adsorption energies and atomistic potential‐energy surfaces is now mature, with errors of tens of meV relative to the reference DFT calculations and accelerations of three orders of magnitude over DFT, yet experimentally validated catalyst improvements remain rare. The most significant advance is the closed‐loop autonomous laboratory coupling Bayesian optimization, automated synthesis and high‐throughput testing. Large language models have begun to add a reasoning and orchestration layer, while kinetics, reactor and process design remain the least digitalized stages. We argue that the field's next decade of impact will be decided not by more accurate atomic‐scale prediction but by carrying ML into experimental validation and the reactor‐and‐process scale, where catalysis is hardest to industrialize and where data‐driven methods are weakest.

items.title: From Automation to Augmentation: Artificial Intelligence, Competence Evolution, and Career Sustainability in the Accounting Profession
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the content of accounting work, but the career consequences of that change remain less clear in emerging economies. Using field responses from 600 accounting and finance professionals in Nigeria, Ghana, and Kenya (200 per country), this paper examines whether intensive AI use is associated with professional role transformation, whether role transformation is associated with competence evolution, and whether those evolving competencies are linked to career sustainability. Learning and organizational support is considered both as a contextual resource and as a potential moderator. The analysis uses multi-item composite measures, HC3-robust path regressions, 5,000-resample bootstrapping, effect-size estimates, 10-fold cross-validation, and exploratory country comparisons. AI adoption was positively associated with role transformation (β = .491, p < .001). AI adoption (β = .286, p < .001) and role transformation (β = .462, p < .001) jointly explained 42.6% of the variance in competence evolution, while competence evolution was positively associated with career sustainability (β = .414, p < .001). The direct role-transformation effect on career sustainability was negligible (β = .013, p = .764), whereas the indirect effect through competence evolution was significant (β = .192, 95% bootstrap CI [.146, .242]). The serial pathway from AI adoption through role transformation and competence evolution to career sustainability was also significant (β = .094, 95% CI [.069, .123]). Learning and organizational support had a positive main effect but did not moderate the competence-sustainability relationship. The results suggest that the long-term value of AI-related role change depends less on the fact that work changes than on whether professionals acquire the digital, analytical, advisory, and ethical capabilities needed to succeed in the redesigned role. Keywords: artificial intelligence; accounting profession; role transformation; competence evolution; career sustainability; emerging economies; Africa; human capital.

items.title: From awareness to trust: a social work perspective on occupational accident rights, employee voice, and safety performance
items.abstract: This study examines the associations among occupational health and safety awareness, OHS performance, employee voice, and organizational trust from a social work perspective. Although previous studies have examined occupational health and safety, employee voice, and organizational trust separately, limited attention has been paid to how these variables operate together within a rights-based and empowerment-oriented social work framework. Data collected from 400 factory employees were analyzed using correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, and PROCESS Model 6. The findings showed that greater awareness was significantly associated with organizational trust through both direct and indirect pathways. OHS performance and employee voice were significant mediators, and the sequential indirect effect through OHS performance and employee voice was statistically significant. Rather than introducing previously unexamined associations, the study integrates established workplace variables within a sequential model and interprets their combined relevance for rights-based education, employee participation, and workplace social work practice.

items.title: From Data to Decision-Making: A Review of Large Language Model Applications Across the Full Lifecycle of Geothermal Resource Development
items.abstract: Geothermal resource development involves heterogeneous geological and engineering records, uncertain reservoir parameters, and decisions constrained by physical processes and safety requirements. This narrative and critical review examines how large language models (LLMs), including retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted systems, could support knowledge-intensive tasks throughout geothermal exploration, development, and operation. It distinguishes direct geothermal evidence from empirical evaluations in adjacent fields and from conceptual proposals; results from petroleum engineering, mineral exploration, and broader energy systems are not treated as proof of geothermal performance. Peer-reviewed studies demonstrate useful capabilities in technical document extraction, domain question answering, knowledge-graph reasoning, and interactions with scientific software, but direct geothermal engineering validation remains limited. For reservoir inversion, drilling-risk warning, and design optimization, quantitative assessment must rely on measured data and validated physical or numerical models, with LLMs acting as auditable interfaces and information-integration tools. The review proposes a task-specific benchmark framework and examines cross-domain transfer, multimodal alignment, knowledge-graph and retrieval collaboration, uncertainty quantification, and LLM–physical-model coupling. These frameworks are literature-informed proposals rather than implemented geothermal systems. Key priorities include independent geothermal test sets, expert-annotated reference answers, calibrated uncertainty, physics-based verification, and transparent reporting of model failure. The resulting synthesis identifies credible current applications and the evidence requirements for reliable future deployment.

items.title: From Natural Equality to Constitutional Legitimacy: Locke’s Political Anthropology and Algorithmic Governance
items.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence into governance challenges the conditions under which political authority can be considered legitimate. Algorithmic systems increasingly mediate decisions that shape citizens’ lives, yet their operations frequently bypass human judgment and obscure the justificatory basis of political authority. This article reinterprets John Locke’s political philosophy as a normative framework for assessing algorithmic authority. By reconstructing Locke’s account of reason, equality, consent, and fiduciary trust, it brings his political anthropology into dialogue with contemporary debates on algorithmic accountability and digital constitutionalism. The article argues that AI governance does not merely raise technical or regulatory problems; it threatens the conditions under which citizens can understand, evaluate, and contest the exercise of power. Because many AI systems operate through models that neither officials nor citizens can meaningfully interpret, they generate forms of automated prerogative that weaken the fiduciary relationship between governors and governed. Against this danger, the article advances a Lockean criterion for computational governance: algorithmic authority can be considered legitimate only insofar as it preserves intelligibility, fiduciary accountability, and contestability. Legitimacy cannot be restored through technical adjustment alone; it requires institutional conditions under which power remains publicly intelligible, politically answerable, and open to challenge by those subject to it.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: From Noisy Retrieval to Decision Evidence: Silver Evidence Demonstrations for In-Context Learning
items.abstract: RAG and retrieval-augmented few-shot ICL can struggle when decision-relevant evidence is buried in long, noisy context. Retrieved passages and demonstrations may contain redundant or distracting information. Although expert-labeled development examples may identify the text supporting each decision, these annotations are typically used only as answer-side rationales rather than as supervision for filtering noisy retrieval. We propose silver-evidence demonstrations, which replace raw retrieved passages in ICL examples with generated, target-conditioned evidence summaries. For each labeled development example, an LLM generates silver evidence without access to the expert label or gold evidence; this evidence is then paired with the expert label and gold evidence where available. At test time, a single structured call generates silver evidence from retrieved passages and then predicts the final label and decision evidence. Across EI 2.0, SciFact, synthetic policy retrieval, and HICRIC/IMR data, our full method improves over equally sized gold-only ICL (label-only for policy) on three of four datasets and improves evidence F1 on all annotated datasets. It also achieves higher mean label accuracy than InstructRAG-style ICL on all four datasets. These results suggest that replacing demonstration-side retrieved passages with compact, target-conditioned silver evidence is particularly useful for decisions based on long and noisy text, where it reduces distracting context while preserving decision-relevant signals and expert supervision.

items.title: From Policy to Pedagogy: A Scoping Review of Artificial Intelligence Implementation Frameworks in Africa Universities
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly influencing higher education through its potential to support teaching, learning, assessment, research, and academic administration. Across Africa, AI offers opportunities to improve educational access, personalise learning, strengthen research capacity, and develop digital competencies. However, realising these benefits requires policies and implementation frameworks that address ethical use, academic integrity, data protection, infrastructure, digital inequalities, and staff and student competencies. The African Union’s Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy provides a continental direction for responsible, inclusive, and development-orientated AI adoption, while the African Union’s Digital Education Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023–2028 support the broader integration of digital technologies into education (African Union, 2024a, 2022).

items.title: From print to algorithm: teaching Indonesian postcolonial fiction with critical algorithmic literacy
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how Indonesian postcolonial fiction – principally Pramoedya Ananta Toer's Bumi Manusia [This Earth of Mankind] and Laksmi Pamuntjak's Amba – was taught across print, digitised and algorithmically mediated environments in two undergraduate English Language Teaching (ELT) literature courses in Surakarta and Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and what teaching critical algorithmic literacy looks like in such courses.Design/methodology/approach A qualitative multiple-case study drew on Indonesian postcolonial criticism, cultural memory studies and work on algorithmic and AI literacy, distinguishing three layers of mediation: digitised reading, algorithmic curation and generative AI. Data comprised classroom observation, instructor interviews, student focus groups and interviews, reflective journals and student-produced ‘feed audits’, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis by an author team that includes the courses’ own teacher.Findings Print-first close reading supported textual warranting and cultural-memory work; students perceived recommendation panels as foregrounding Anglophone titles over Indonesian ones; instructor-designed counter-searches and feed audits made algorithmic curation an object of critique; digital tools supported translanguaging across Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and English when paired with evaluation criteria; and hybrid sequencing was valued but labour-intensive.Originality/value The study's innovation is pedagogical rather than technological: a resource-aware, print-first sequence of feed audits, Indonesian-language counter-searches, checklists for generative AI output and evidence ladders that turns algorithms into objects of literary inquiry. It brings Indonesian literary criticism and language politics into dialogue with algorithmic literacy and identifies the conditions under which such teaching may be sustainable in Indonesian higher education.

items.title: From Promises to Accountability: Comparative AI Modeling and Visualization of Electoral Commitments in Nepali Political Texts
items.abstract: Election Commitment Mining refers to the analysis of election commitments made by electoral candidates or political parties during election campaigns. However, many elected candidates and political parties, especially in developing South Asian countries, do not fully deliver on the promises they make before elections. Even after the elections, commitments presented through election manifestos, posters, pamphlets, videos, and other campaign materials are often not systematically or transparently archived. As a result, these promises tend to fade away over time, making it difficult to hold the elected candidates accountable for their commitments. To address this persistent issue, this research aims to develop a system capable of structuring the commitments made by candidates during election periods. In this work, we created the first gold-standard dataset of Nepali political texts (Cohen's kappa = 0.777) and evaluated machine learning, deep learning and large language models to automatically extract and analyze election commitments. LaBSE-LR achieved the best results among machine learning models (0.897 accuracy, 0.896 macro F1-score, 0.947 AUROC), while fastText-LSTM achieved the highest performance among deep learning models (0.914 accuracy, 0.913 macro F1-score, 0.961 AUROC). Among the three evaluated large language models, Qwen3-8B performed best in the few-shot setting (0.848 macro F1-score). The outcome of this work is integrated into a mobile application, where commitments can be visualized with the support of GAI, enhancing transparency, civic engagement, and electoral accountability.

items.title: From Responsible Leadership to Responsible AI Governance: A Leadership-Based Framework for AI Governance in Organizations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational decision-making, managerial roles, and accountability, yet responsible AI governance remains dominated by principles, technical controls, and regulatory compliance. This conceptual paper develops a human leadership-based framework for translating responsible AI principles into organizational governance. In the framework, the responsible leader is an accountable human organizational actor—such as a board member, senior executive, business leader, or designated decision owner—while AI is treated as a governed technological system or operational agent rather than the accountable leader. Human responsible leadership influences responsible AI governance (RAIG) capability through six mediating organizational processes: stakeholder orientation, ethical sensemaking, accountability architecture, meaningful human oversight, inclusive participation, and long-term value orientation. RAIG capability is defined as the higher-order organizational capacity to institutionalize and adapt lifecycle governance arrangements; it enables observable governance practices, which are conceptually separated from downstream responsible AI outcomes. AI operational autonomy is proposed as a focal moderator: the leadership-to-RAIG pathway should become stronger when AI can initiate or execute consequential actions with limited contemporaneous human approval, particularly where actions are difficult to reverse, trace, or interrupt. The framework offers testable propositions and a research agenda, but it is conceptual and requires empirical validation; it is not a technical safety guarantee.

items.title: From simulation to pedagogy: multi-model and randomized evaluation of structured AI standardized patients
items.abstract: Standardized patients (SPs) are central to clinical communication training but remain constrained by cost, scalability, and reliance on trained actors. We present AI standardized patients (AI-SPs), large language model–driven patient simulators built on a three-layer information architecture that adaptively modulates information disclosure according to learner skill. In Phase 1, blinded expert assessment of 350 simulated consultations generated by five frontier LLMs showed that, under a common architecture, learner skill level accounted for more of the observed performance variation than model choice ( η 2 = 0.31 vs. 0.06); whether this reflects the architecture itself cannot be determined without comparing models with and without it. In Phase 1b, analysis of 155 live student consultations identified systematic failures to elicit safety-critical information, enabling automated curriculum diagnostics without expert observation. In a Phase 2 three-arm pilot randomized study ( n = 58), OSCE performance gains with AI-SP training did not differ significantly from those with human SP training; the trial was designed to estimate effect sizes for a future confirmatory study, not to demonstrate equivalence. Self-efficacy gains were numerically largest with AI-SP training, but this exploratory difference did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. These findings suggest that architecture-driven AI-SPs could provide a scalable, model-portable approach to clinical communication training.

items.title: From Technology Readiness to Technical Competence
items.abstract: Purpose: The digital transformation in accounting, driven by automation and artificial intelligence, has reinforced the importance of technical skills, particularly in terms of technological adaptation in the training of future professionals. In this context, this study analyses the relation between the technological readiness of higher education students and their perception of technical readiness across the 12 competency areas operationalised from the International Education Standard 2 (IES 2) of the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC). Method: The research adopts a quantitative approach, based on a structured questionnaire administered to 146 students. The survey comprised three core components: sociodemographic data, self-assessment of technical readiness across the 12 IES 2 competency areas, and application of the Technology Readiness Index (TRI 2.0). Data analysis involved descriptive statistics, reliability analysis and Spearman’s correlations, with the aim of examining the association between technological readiness and the perception of technical competencies. Main Results: Based on the TRI 2.0 model by Parasuraman and Colby (2015), the results reveal a profile characterised by high optimism, moderate innovativeness, relatively low discomfort and high insecurity, reflecting a moderate overall level of technological readiness. At the same time, students report an overall positive perception of their technical readiness, with higher scores in financial accounting and reporting, information and communication technologies, and taxation, and lower scores in auditing. However, no statistically significant association was observed between overall technological readiness and the overall perception of technical competence. Nevertheless, a positive and significant relation was identified between overall technological readiness and competence in information and communication technologies. Key Conclusions: It is concluded that technological readiness does not automatically translate into a high overall perception of technical competence, although it appears to be associated with areas more directly related to the use of technology. The results reinforce the importance of pedagogical strategies that link the development of technical skills with technological adaptation, in a professional context increasingly marked by technological demands.

items.title: From the Soul Life of the Creator to the Black Box of the AI Chatbot: How to Close the Attribution Gap of AI Output?
items.abstract: Abstract This article addresses the profound legal dilemma posed by Generative AI within the contemporary art scene, arguing that German copyright law must focus not only on the work’s inherent object qualities but in particular on the human’s demonstrable concrete control over the output. When artists input hyper-complex prompt chains into AI tools like Midjourney or DALL-E to generate a picture, the essential question arises: Who owns the result? This legal challenge is twofold: an attribution crisis and a transparency crisis. Because the AI autonomously produces works without the required link to a human author’s personality, it creates a fundamental attribution gap. The challenge is no longer merely about the work itself, but about establishing a verifiable human influence amid the AI’s ‘black box’ processes. This analysis explores this critical question by examining the chain of attribution across three distinct stages of human influence over the AI process: Architecture/Training Data (Upstream), Prompting (Direct), and Post-processing (Downstream).
